 Centre Scraps Petrol Export Levy, Hikes Diesel Duty to Rs 11.5 Per Litre 
 By Kavita Iyer 
 Oct 31, 2026 
 No Comments 
 New Delhi, October 31: India’s fuel export tax structure just got reshuffled, and the timing, the last day of October, feels deliberate. The Centre has zeroed out the levy on petrol exports, raised the duty on diesel exports to Rs 11.5 per litre, and nudged the aviation turbine fuel rate up slightly to Rs 11 per litre. All of it published in the Official Gazette on Friday, all of it in force from today.
 On paper, these are just numbers in a government notification. In practice, they say quite a lot about where global energy markets are right now, and how uncomfortable the Centre remains about India’s fuel supply security.
 The Actual Numbers, Without the Jargon 
 The Special Additional Excise Duty , or SAED , is what the government uses to tax fuel exports. Friday’s revision did three things at once.
 Petrol export duty: gone. It was Rs 2.5 per litre as recently as October 16. Now it is nil.
 Diesel export duty: up sharply. From Rs 8.5 per litre to Rs 11.5 per litre, a Rs 3 jump in a single fortnight.
 ATF export duty: nudged up. From Rs 10.5 to Rs 11 per litre.
 Two separate notifications from the Department of Revenue under the Ministry of Finance cover these changes. Both are effective October 31, 2026.
 Go Back to March to Understand Why Any of This Exists 
 The SAED on fuel exports was not always part of the picture. The Centre introduced it on March 27, 2026 , specifically in response to the West Asia crisis , which by that point had rattled global energy supply chains badly enough that the government felt it needed a new kind of lever.
 The worry was not complicated. Indian refiners, responding to strong margins abroad, were finding it more profitable to export petrol, diesel and ATF than to sell them domestically. The government’s concern was that this could quietly drain domestic fuel availability, especially for diesel, which keeps trucks moving, farms running and freight flowing across the country.
 Slapping an export duty on these fuels was the chosen fix. Not a price cap, not rationing, just a financial disincentive that made exporting slightly less attractive. The mechanism was designed to be adjusted, not fixed. Since March, the rates have been reviewed every fortnight , based on how international crude and refined product prices have moved in the preceding two weeks.
 Petrol and Diesel Are Moving in Opposite Directions, and That Is the Story 
 The interesting thing about Friday’s revision is not any single number. It is the direction in which petrol and diesel are moving simultaneously, because they are going opposite ways, and that gap tells you everything.
 Petrol getting zeroed out is a signal that the government no longer feels the need to discourage petrol exports. International petrol prices relative to domestic margins have shifted to the point where refiners are not rushing to export. Domestic supply is holding. The levy did its job, and it has been quietly retired for now.
 Diesel getting hammered with a Rs 3 hike tells a different story entirely. Diesel is not just another fuel in India. It is the fuel that powers the economy at its most basic level, and any supply squeeze shows up fast in freight rates, food prices and farm operations. The fact that the Centre has raised the diesel levy this aggressively suggests global diesel prices are still attractive enough that refiners are tempted to ship it out rather than sell it here. The government is closing that gap, firmly.
 The ATF adjustment is modest but deliberate. Indian aviation has bounced back, domestic passenger numbers are strong, and airlines are extremely sensitive to fuel cost changes. A Rs 0.50 per litre increase in ATF export duty is not going to shock anyone, but it signals that the Centre wants to keep domestic jet fuel supply well-stocked as winter travel volumes build.
 The Fortnight Cycle Is the Whole Point 
 What often gets missed in the coverage of these SAED revisions is how the review mechanism itself works, and why it matters.
 Every two weeks, the government looks at average international prices for crude oil, petrol, diesel and ATF. If global prices for refined products have risen and exporters are finding better returns abroad, the duty goes up to discourage outflows. If prices have softened and domestic supply is running comfortably, the duty comes down or gets zeroed out.
 This is what happened with petrol today. It has also happened with diesel before, going up and down across multiple revisions since March. The rates have changed several times since the system was introduced, each revision reflecting where the market was in the preceding fortnight.
 It is a flexible mechanism, which is genuinely smart policy design. Changing regular excise duties requires Parliamentary approval and is a slow, unwieldy process. The SAED can be revised through gazette notifications, which is why the government can move every two weeks instead of waiting months for a budget cycle.
 That said, the flexibility cuts both ways. For businesses that operate on longer planning horizons, fleet operators, airlines, large agricultural users, a rate environment that can shift every two weeks is genuinely hard to plan around. Fuel cost projections become guesswork. Hedging strategies have a short shelf life.
 What It Means for Refiners 
 India’s large refining companies run some of the most complex operations in Asia. They buy crude internationally, process it domestically, and then make decisions about how to sell the output based on where margins are better, at home or in export markets.
 When global refined product prices are strong, exporting generates better returns. The SAED directly cuts into those export margins, pulling the economics back toward domestic sales. A sharply higher diesel levy, therefore, is a message to refiners: keep more of your diesel output for the Indian market.
 The petrol exemption, on the other hand, gives refiners room to move petrol overseas if global prices are favourable. For companies running on tight margins across a portfolio of products, that flexibility on petrol partially offsets the tighter constraints on diesel.
 India’s Energy Security Arithmetic Has Not Changed 
 The West Asia crisis has kept global energy markets volatile for months now. Shipping disruptions, crude supply uncertainty, and sharp swings in refined product prices have forced every major oil-importing country to rethink how it protects domestic supply.
 India imports the bulk of its crude. Its vulnerability to global price shocks is structural. The SAED is designed to be one part of the response: a fast-acting, regularly calibrated tool that the government can use to keep domestic fuel supply intact without resorting to price controls or direct interventions, which would be far more disruptive for the market.
 The trade-off is the uncertainty it creates for industry. The government appears to have decided that trade-off is worth it. Keeping diesel on Indian shelves matters more, right now, than making life simpler for refinery finance teams.
 What Happens Next 
 The next SAED review is roughly two weeks away. If global diesel prices pull back, the duty may ease. If ATF demand from overseas buyers firms up, the Rs 11 per litre levy might hold or climb further. Petrol’s zero rate could come back if domestic supply tightens again.
 None of it is permanent. All of it is tied to where international prices land in the next fortnight. That is the nature of the mechanism, and at this point, refiners, airlines and freight operators have had since March to get used to it.
 What the October 31 revision confirms is that the global energy situation remains unsettled enough that the government is still watching these markets closely, twice a month, and adjusting accordingly. For an economy as dependent on diesel as India’s, that vigilance is not overcaution. It is exactly what the moment requires.
